title: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament

paper.title: When Rewards Depend on the Group, GRPO Plays a Tournament
paper.abstract: Abstract Rewards for diversity, coverage and distribution matching make the reward of each sampled response depend on the rest of its group, and they are now routinely optimized with GRPO and RLOO. We prove that in this setting the group-relative baseline changes the objective. The expected update equals each response’s own reward gradient plus α \alpha times its effect on its groupmates’ rewards, with α = − 1 / ( K − 1 ) \alpha=-1/(K-1) for groups of size K K , so GRPO trains every response to beat its groupmates in a zero-sum tournament. It cannot see a pairwise diversity bonus when K = 2 K=2 , sees less than half of it at any K K , and often does worse than using no baseline at all. Setting α = + 1 \alpha=+1 gives Team-GRPO, an unbiased estimator for any group-dependent reward that works with two samples per prompt and requires no extra model calls for pairwise rewards. The theory predicts training quantitatively. It locates the fixed points of a 9B policy to within 0.02 0.02 in ℓ 1 \ell_{1} and predicts how concentrated trained policies become with Pearson r = 0.995 r=0.995 . On GlobalOpinionQA, GRPO collapses onto the majority answer and ends further from human opinion than the untrained model, while Team-GRPO cuts the error from 0.20 0.20 to 0.08 0.08 . On NoveltyBench, Team-GRPO avoids the diversity collapse of GRPO and significantly improves set utility.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Group-relative policy gradients are the default way to fine-tune language models with reinforcement learning. GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and RLOO ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) sample K K responses per prompt and score each against the mean reward of its group, which removes the need for a learned critic ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025c ) . The justification is classical ( Williams, 1992 ; Greensmith et al., 2004 ) . When the reward of a response depends only on that response, its groupmates’ rewards are independent of it, so subtracting their mean lowers variance without changing the expected update. A fast-growing family of rewards breaks this assumption. To counter the loss of diversity under reinforcement learning ( Kirk et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2025 ) , DARLING multiplies each response’s quality by its semantic distance to its groupmates ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and other methods add pairwise novelty bonuses ( Song et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) or reward answers that are rare within the group ( Anschel et al., 2025 ) . Distributional alignment penalizes collisions with groupmates so that the group reproduces a target distribution ( Arabi et al., 2026 ) , and set-level objectives score the group as a whole ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Orney et al., 2026 ) . In each case the reward of response k k depends on the whole group, so its baseline depends on it through its groupmates’ rewards, and the classical argument fails. Figure 1 : The problem. An answer helps its group by being good and by being different. GRPO credits each sample with how far it beats the group mean, so groupmates become rivals and converge on one answer. Team-GRPO credits each sample with what it adds to the group, so the group stays diverse. We show that the result is not extra noise but a different objective. For any reward that treats groupmates symmetrically, the expected GRPO update is the gradient of a response’s own reward plus α \alpha times its externality , the change it causes in its groupmates’ rewards, with α = − 1 / ( K − 1 ) \alpha=-1/(K-1) ( Theorem 1 ). The true gradient counts the externality with weight + 1 +1 , so subtracting the group mean does not merely discard it but reverses its sign. GRPO trains each response to beat its groupmates, a zero-sum tournament like the relative-payoff game that governs selection in finite populations ( Schaffer, 1988 ) , in which groupmates are rivals rather than a team ( Figure 1 ). The tournament has closed-form consequences ( Figure 2 ). A pairwise diversity bonus reaches the update with ( K − 2 ) / ( 2 ​ ( K − 1 ) ) (K-2)/(2(K-1)) of its true weight, which is below one half for every K K and zero at K = 2 K=2 , where GRPO cannot tell two different good answers from one good answer given twice. Larger groups do not rescue it, because as K K grows GRPO approaches REINFORCE without a baseline rather than the optimum of the reward. Across six reward structures from recent methods, GRPO is never better than REINFORCE and is often far worse. Setting α = + 1 \alpha=+1 restores the true gradient. The resulting estimator, Team-GRPO, credits each response with its marginal contribution to the group’s reward, using only quantities the reward already computes ( Section 3 ). It works with two samples per prompt, an efficient regime ( Wu et al., 2025 ) in which GRPO fails completely, and it contains recent special-purpose estimators for max@ k k ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Takashiro et al., 2026 ) , distribution matching ( Arabi et al., 2026 ) and set-level reinforcement learning ( Orney et al., 2026 ) as special cases. Figure 2 : GRPO plays a tournament. (a) Team-GRPO maximizes the group’s total reward, REINFORCE without a baseline maximizes each response’s own reward (a Nash equilibrium), and GRPO maximizes each response’s reward minus the mean of its groupmates’ (a zero-sum tournament). Bars give the weight of a pairwise diversity bonus in the expected update relative to the true gradient ( Corollary 2 ). (b) Two responses of quality q = 0.8 q=0.8 under the reward q ⁡ ( 1 + λ ​ d ) q\,(1+\lambda d) , λ = 2 \lambda=2 . GRPO assigns zero advantage whether the answers differ ( d = 1 d=1 ) or coincide ( d = 0 d=0 ). Team-GRPO separates the two cases. (c) Answer shares on a held-out GlobalOpinionQA question (whether the gap between rich and poor has grown, Venezuela) after 200 steps with two samples per question. The theory makes quantitative predictions, each fixed before the corresponding experiment. In a sandbox where the policy of a 9B model can be read off exactly, all 12 runs with a closed-form prediction converge to the fixed point of their estimator’s game (largest ℓ 1 \ell_{1} error 0.018 0.018 ). On GlobalOpinionQA ( Durmus et al., 2024 ) , the theory predicted that GRPO with two samples per question would collapse onto the majority answer and end worse than the untrained model. It did, raising the squared error to the human distribution from 0.20 0.20 to 0.49 0.49 , while Team-GRPO lowers it to 0.08 0.08 . Across 13 configurations the closed-form fixed points predict how concentrated the trained policy becomes with Pearson r = 0.995 r=0.995 . On NoveltyBench ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) with a quality-times-diversity reward, GRPO collapses in every seed, whereas Team-GRPO keeps the model diverse and raises set utility over GRPO by 1.16 1.16 at K = 2 K=2 and 0.56 0.56 at K = 8 K=8 , gains that persist at matched KL divergence and under an independent LLM judge.

sections.heading: Contributions.
sections.text: • Diagnosis. An exact identity for group-relative estimators under any exchangeable group reward, its reading as a relative-payoff game, and its closed-form consequences ( Section 2 ). • Method. Team-GRPO, an unbiased and essentially free estimator for any exchangeable group reward that works at K = 2 K=2 and unifies recent special-purpose estimators ( Section 3 ). • Evidence. Quantitative confirmation on a 9B model in distributional alignment and open-ended generation, where Team-GRPO outperforms GRPO and its variants and matches set-level estimators wherever they apply ( Section 4 ).

sections.text: Give player k k of a symmetric K K -player game the payoff U k α = r k + α ​ ∑ j ≠ k r j U^{\alpha}_{k}=r_{k}+\alpha\sum_{j\neq k}r_{j} . sections.heading: Which weight is intended.
sections.text: The diagnosis does not rest on taking J J as the target. A designer may want each response credited for its total effect on the group ( α = 1 \alpha=1 ) or for its own reward against fixed groupmates ( α = 0 \alpha=0 ), but never for lowering its groupmates’ rewards. GRPO’s α \alpha is negative at every K K , so it serves neither intention, and at K = 2 K=2 it gives a pairwise diversity bonus zero weight where both give it positive weight. The methods we study intend α = 1 \alpha=1 , since each is evaluated by a property of the whole set, such as pass@ k k , coverage or distance to a target distribution ( Table 9 ). For α = 0 \alpha=0 the same construction gives an unbiased estimator ( Section A.7 ).

sections.heading: Normalization and variance.
sections.text: As in Dr. GRPO and DARLING we do not divide by the group’s standard deviation ( Appendix E ). At matched scale the variance of Team-GRPO is 1.1 1.1 – 2.1 2.1 times that of RLOO for K ≥ 4 K\geq 4 ( Appendix C ). sections.heading: 4 Experiments
sections.text: We test whether the theory predicts where training converges, whether the tournament hurts across reward structures in current use, and whether Team-GRPO yields better models in distributional alignment and open-ended generation. Unless stated otherwise we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B ( Qwen Team, 2026 ) with rank-16 LoRA ( Hu et al., 2022 ) at temperature 1, with a sequence-level policy-gradient loss, a constant normalizer, no KL penalty and no standard-deviation normalization, identically for all estimators. Each batch is used for one on-policy update, where importance ratios equal one and the clipped surrogate of PPO and GRPO has exactly this gradient (normalization and clipping with several epochs are tested in Appendices E and F ). Confidence intervals are 95%, from a paired bootstrap over prompts or a t t -interval across seeds.

sections.heading: GRPO trains a quality-only policy.
sections.text: At K = 2 K=2 the GRPO advantage ( 5 ) ignores diversity, and in all three seeds the trained model has fewer distinct answers and lower utility than the base model. Averaged over seeds, distinct answers fall from 4.33 4.33 to 2.65 2.65 and utility from 4.01 4.01 to 3.44 3.44 , while first-sample quality rises from 7.58 7.58 to 9.04 9.04 ( Table 3 , Figure 5 a,b). This rise is the predicted signature of the failure, not a strength. A policy that sees only quality moves its mass onto its single best answer, which raises the score of any one sample while the set collapses. Team-GRPO makes the trade the reward asks for, giving up 0.53 0.53 points of single-sample quality to win on both set metrics.

sections.heading: Team-GRPO optimizes the set.
sections.text: Under the same reward, Team-GRPO keeps the model diverse ( 4.56 4.56 distinct answers) and raises utility to 4.61 4.61 , significantly above both the base model and GRPO ( + 1.16 +1.16 [ 0.52 , 1.80 ] [0.52,1.80] over GRPO). GRPO drifts further from the base model (sequence KL 123 123 against 54 54 ), so we also evaluate GRPO at the KL each Team-GRPO run reaches at step 150, where Team-GRPO still leads by + 0.84 +0.84 [ 0.79 , 0.90 ] [0.79,0.90] in utility and + 1.12 +1.12 [ 0.46 , 1.79 ] [0.46,1.79] in distinct answers ( Figure 5 c). Single prompts show the difference plainly. Asked to pick a random prime between 1 and 50, GRPO answers 23 in seven of ten samples, while Team-GRPO names six different primes ( Table 16 ).

sections.heading: An independent judge agrees.
sections.text: The training reward model and the benchmark scorer both come from the Skywork family, so we also apply the NoveltyBench v1.1 protocol, in which an external language model (Claude Sonnet 5.5) groups and scores the samples, to a random subset of 100 prompts ( Table 13 ). Team-GRPO beats GRPO in utility and distinct answers at both group sizes, by + 0.61 +0.61 and + 2.09 +2.09 at K = 2 K=2 and by + 0.26 +0.26 and + 1.34 +1.34 at K = 8 K=8 , all with intervals excluding zero, and it is the only trained model above the base model on both set metrics. The differences remain positive at matched KL, and as under the benchmark scorer GRPO’s first sample scores higher while its set scores lower.

sections.heading: Baselines and credit assignment.
sections.text: Baselines reduce variance without bias as long as they do not depend on the action ( Williams, 1992 ; Greensmith et al., 2004 ) . Leave-one-out and group-mean baselines ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) made critic-free training standard for language models, and later work examined their normalization and length bias ( Liu et al., 2025c ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Vojnovic & Yun, 2025 ) . Action-dependent baselines need a correction to stay unbiased ( Tucker et al., 2018 ; Wu et al., 2018 ) , and the bias we characterize is of this kind, entering through the groupmates’ rewards. Counterfactual baselines ( Foerster et al., 2018 ) and difference rewards ( Wolpert & Tumer, 2001 ) credit each agent with its marginal contribution, and Team-GRPO applies this idea to samples of one policy, where the counterfactual is exact. Multi-agent GRPO variants with baselines from independent episodes ( Liu et al., 2025b ) are unaffected. Selection in finite populations maximizes relative payoff and can reward spite ( Schaffer, 1988 ; Nowak et al., 2004 ; Hamilton, 1970 ; Vega-Redondo, 1997 ) , as tournament contracts do ( Lazear & Rosen, 1981 ; Lazear, 1989 ) .

sections.heading: Group-dependent rewards.
sections.text: Diversity methods reward semantic distinctness, embedding distance or rarity within the group ( Li et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Anschel et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . Distributional and pluralistic alignment ask a policy to match a population of views ( Durmus et al., 2024 ; Sorensen et al., 2024 ; Arabi et al., 2026 ) , and set-level objectives target pass@ k k ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Takashiro et al., 2026 ) , strategy coverage ( Orney et al., 2026 ; Hamid et al., 2026 ) , marginal diversity ( Li et al., 2026 ) or within-group preferences ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Most feed the group-dependent reward into the standard advantage, and GAPO argues explicitly that this is unbiased because the reward does not contain θ \theta ( Anschel et al., 2025 ) . Our analysis shows that the estimator then plays a tournament, and it gives one correction that also holds in the small groups favored for efficiency ( Wu et al., 2025 ) .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: Group-relative baselines were introduced to reduce variance. When the reward depends on the group they also change the game, from a team effort into a tournament in which every response is rewarded for beating its groupmates. The change hides diversity from two-sample training, keeps less than half of any pairwise bonus, drives distribution matching toward the majority answer, and leaves a bias that larger groups do not remove. Counting each response’s externality with the right sign restores the true gradient at every group size, without additional model calls for pairwise rewards.

sections.heading: Impact Statement
sections.text: This work concerns how reinforcement-learning objectives for language models are optimized when rewards depend on several sampled responses at once. Rewards of this kind are used to keep models diverse, to represent the spread of human opinion rather than its majority, and to cover many valid answers. We show that the standard estimator quietly works against these goals and provide a corrected estimator. A model trained toward a population’s opinion distribution reproduces that distribution, including its disagreements, so practitioners should choose target populations with care. We see no other societal consequence that needs to be highlighted here.

sections.heading: Appendix E Standard-deviation normalization
sections.text: Standard GRPO divides each advantage by the standard deviation of the group’s rewards. At K = 2 K=2 this keeps only the sign of r 1 − r 2 r_{1}-r_{2} , in which a symmetric pairwise term cancels, so normalization inherits GRPO’s blindness exactly, sample by sample. Normalization moves the fixed point by up to 0.19 0.19 , and the trained 9B policies land within 0.01 0.01 of the numerical prediction at K = 4 K=4 and K = 8 K=8 . sections.heading: Data.
sections.text: We use the GlobalOpinionQA release of Durmus et al. (2024) . For each (question, country) pair we drop non-substantive options (“Don’t know”, “Refused” and similar), renormalize the rest, and keep items with at least two options and at least half of the mass on substantive options. We split by question text with 70% of questions for training, 10% for development and 20% for testing, and keep at most three countries per question in the development and test splits. This yields 32,372 training items, 618 development items and 1,154 test items. The prompt reads “Imagine you are a randomly selected adult living in [country], answering a public opinion survey.”, followed by the question, the lettered options, and the instruction to reply with the letter only.

We prove that in this setting the group-relative baseline changes the objective. The expected update equals each response’s own reward gradient plus α \alpha times its effect on its groupmates’ rewards, with α = − 1 / ( K − 1 ) \alpha=-1/(K-1) for groups of size K K , so GRPO trains every response to beat its groupmates in a zero-sum tournament. It cannot see a pairwise diversity bonus when K = 2 K=2 , sees less than half of it at any K K , and often does worse than using no baseline at all. Setting α = + 1 \alpha=+1 gives Team-GRPO, an unbiased estimator for any group-dependent reward that works with two samples per prompt and requires no extra model calls for pairwise rewards. The theory predicts training quantitatively. It locates the fixed points of a 9B policy to within 0.02 0.02 in ℓ 1 \ell_{1} and predicts how concentrated trained policies become with Pearson r = 0.995 r=0.995 . On GlobalOpinionQA, GRPO collapses onto the majority answer and ends further from human opinion than the untrained model, while Team-GRPO cuts the error from 0.20 0.20 to 0.08 0.08 . On NoveltyBench, Team-GRPO avoids the diversity collapse of GRPO and significantly improves set utility. Keywords: reinforcement learning, policy gradient, GRPO, credit assignment, diversity, language models Junyi Gao 1,3,* Yu Shi 2,* Pingzhao Hu 4,† Ewen M Harrison 1,† 1 Centre for Medical Informatics, University of Edinburgh 2 Biostatistics Division, Dalla Lana School of Public Health, University of Toronto 3 Health Data Research UK 4 Department of Biochemistry, Western University * Equal contribution † Senior author \icml@noticeprintedtrue † † footnotetext: \Notice@String 1 Introduction Group-relative policy gradients are the default way to fine-tune language models with reinforcement learning. GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and RLOO ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) sample K K responses per prompt and score each against the mean reward of its group, which removes the need for a learned critic ( Guo et al., 2025 ; Liu et al., 2025c ) . The justification is classical ( Williams, 1992 ; Greensmith et al., 2004 ) . When the reward of a response depends only on that response, its groupmates’ rewards are independent of it, so subtracting their mean lowers variance without changing the expected update. A fast-growing family of rewards breaks this assumption. To counter the loss of diversity under reinforcement learning ( Kirk et al., 2024 ; Yue et al., 2025 ) , DARLING multiplies each response’s quality by its semantic distance to its groupmates ( Li et al., 2025 ) , and other methods add pairwise novelty bonuses ( Song et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ) or reward answers that are rare within the group ( Anschel et al., 2025 ) . Distributional alignment penalizes collisions with groupmates so that the group reproduces a target distribution ( Arabi et al., 2026 ) , and set-level objectives score the group as a whole ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Orney et al., 2026 ) . In each case the reward of response k k depends on the whole group, so its baseline depends on it through its groupmates’ rewards, and the classical argument fails. Figure 1 : The problem. An answer helps its group by being good and by being different. GRPO credits each sample with how far it beats the group mean, so groupmates become rivals and converge on one answer. Team-GRPO credits each sample with what it adds to the group, so the group stays diverse. We show that the result is not extra noise but a different objective. For any reward that treats groupmates symmetrically, the expected GRPO update is the gradient of a response’s own reward plus α \alpha times its externality , the change it causes in its groupmates’ rewards, with α = − 1 / ( K − 1 ) \alpha=-1/(K-1) ( Theorem 1 ). The true gradient counts the externality with weight + 1 +1 , so subtracting the group mean does not merely discard it but reverses its sign. GRPO trains each response to beat its groupmates, a zero-sum tournament like the relative-payoff game that governs selection in finite populations ( Schaffer, 1988 ) , in which groupmates are rivals rather than a team ( Figure 1 ). The tournament has closed-form consequences ( Figure 2 ). A pairwise diversity bonus reaches the update with ( K − 2 ) / ( 2 ​ ( K − 1 ) ) (K-2)/(2(K-1)) of its true weight, which is below one half for every K K and zero at K = 2 K=2 , where GRPO cannot tell two different good answers from one good answer given twice. Larger groups do not rescue it, because as K K grows GRPO approaches REINFORCE without a baseline rather than the optimum of the reward. Across six reward structures from recent methods, GRPO is never better than REINFORCE and is often far worse. Setting α = + 1 \alpha=+1 restores the true gradient. The resulting estimator, Team-GRPO, credits each response with its marginal contribution to the group’s reward, using only quantities the reward already computes ( Section 3 ). It works with two samples per prompt, an efficient regime ( Wu et al., 2025 ) in which GRPO fails completely, and it contains recent special-purpose estimators for max@ k k ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Takashiro et al., 2026 ) , distribution matching ( Arabi et al., 2026 ) and set-level reinforcement learning ( Orney et al., 2026 ) as special cases. Figure 2 : GRPO plays a tournament. (a) Team-GRPO maximizes the group’s total reward, REINFORCE without a baseline maximizes each response’s own reward (a Nash equilibrium), and GRPO maximizes each response’s reward minus the mean of its groupmates’ (a zero-sum tournament). Bars give the weight of a pairwise diversity bonus in the expected update relative to the true gradient ( Corollary 2 ). (b) Two responses of quality q = 0.8 q=0.8 under the reward q ⁡ ( 1 + λ ​ d ) q\,(1+\lambda d) , λ = 2 \lambda=2 . GRPO assigns zero advantage whether the answers differ ( d = 1 d=1 ) or coincide ( d = 0 d=0 ). Team-GRPO separates the two cases. (c) Answer shares on a held-out GlobalOpinionQA question (whether the gap between rich and poor has grown, Venezuela) after 200 steps with two samples per question. The theory makes quantitative predictions, each fixed before the corresponding experiment. In a sandbox where the policy of a 9B model can be read off exactly, all 12 runs with a closed-form prediction converge to the fixed point of their estimator’s game (largest ℓ 1 \ell_{1} error 0.018 0.018 ). On GlobalOpinionQA ( Durmus et al., 2024 ) , the theory predicted that GRPO with two samples per question would collapse onto the majority answer and end worse than the untrained model. It did, raising the squared error to the human distribution from 0.20 0.20 to 0.49 0.49 , while Team-GRPO lowers it to 0.08 0.08 . Across 13 configurations the closed-form fixed points predict how concentrated the trained policy becomes with Pearson r = 0.995 r=0.995 . On NoveltyBench ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) with a quality-times-diversity reward, GRPO collapses in every seed, whereas Team-GRPO keeps the model diverse and raises set utility over GRPO by 1.16 1.16 at K = 2 K=2 and 0.56 0.56 at K = 8 K=8 , gains that persist at matched KL divergence and under an independent LLM judge. Baselines reduce variance without bias as long as they do not depend on the action ( Williams, 1992 ; Greensmith et al., 2004 ) . Leave-one-out and group-mean baselines ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ; Shao et al., 2024 ) made critic-free training standard for language models, and later work examined their normalization and length bias ( Liu et al., 2025c ; Yu et al., 2025 ; Vojnovic & Yun, 2025 ) . Action-dependent baselines need a correction to stay unbiased ( Tucker et al., 2018 ; Wu et al., 2018 ) , and the bias we characterize is of this kind, entering through the groupmates’ rewards. Counterfactual baselines ( Foerster et al., 2018 ) and difference rewards ( Wolpert & Tumer, 2001 ) credit each agent with its marginal contribution, and Team-GRPO applies this idea to samples of one policy, where the counterfactual is exact. Multi-agent GRPO variants with baselines from independent episodes ( Liu et al., 2025b ) are unaffected. Selection in finite populations maximizes relative payoff and can reward spite ( Schaffer, 1988 ; Nowak et al., 2004 ; Hamilton, 1970 ; Vega-Redondo, 1997 ) , as tournament contracts do ( Lazear & Rosen, 1981 ; Lazear, 1989 ) . Group-dependent rewards. Diversity methods reward semantic distinctness, embedding distance or rarity within the group ( Li et al., 2025 ; Song et al., 2025 ; Wan et al., 2026 ; Anschel et al., 2025 ; Shi et al., 2026 ) . Distributional and pluralistic alignment ask a policy to match a population of views ( Durmus et al., 2024 ; Sorensen et al., 2024 ; Arabi et al., 2026 ) , and set-level objectives target pass@ k k ( Walder & Karkhanis, 2025 ; Takashiro et al., 2026 ) , strategy coverage ( Orney et al., 2026 ; Hamid et al., 2026 ) , marginal diversity ( Li et al., 2026 ) or within-group preferences ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . Most feed the group-dependent reward into the standard advantage, and GAPO argues explicitly that this is unbiased because the reward does not contain θ 	heta ( Anschel et al., 2025 ) . Our analysis shows that the estimator then plays a tournament, and it gives one correction that also holds in the small groups favored for efficiency ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . 6 Conclusion Group-relative baselines were introduced to reduce variance. When the reward depends on the group they also change the game, from a team effort into a tournament in which every response is rewarded for beating its groupmates. The change hides diversity from two-sample training, keeps less than half of any pairwise bonus, drives distribution matching toward the majority answer, and leaves a bias that larger groups do not remove. Counting each response’s externality with the right sign restores the true gradient at every group size, without additional model calls for pairwise rewards. Impact Statement This work concerns how reinforcement-learning objectives for language models are optimized when rewards depend on several sampled responses at once. Rewards of this kind are used to keep models diverse, to represent the spread of human opinion rather than its majority, and to cover many valid answers. We show that the standard estimator quietly works against these goals and provide a corrected estimator. A model trained toward a population’s opinion distribution reproduces that distribution, including its disagreements, so practitioners should choose target populations with care. We see no other societal consequence that needs to be highlighted here. References Ahmadian et al.
